II.1 Emergent accidental symmetries

The irreps degeneracy of the Hamiltonian describing the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line results in the identification of accidental symmetries defining continuous manifolds where the spin configuration can fluctuate with no associated energy cost. Indeed, the simplest low-energy manifold in the ground-state of the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line is associated with the EE irrep; in the Hamiltonian in Eq. (4), the two-dimensional EE irrep takes the form

aE​𝐦E2=aE​[(mEx)2+(mEy)2],a_{E}\mathbf{m}_{E}^{2}=a_{E}\left[(m_{E}^{x})^{2}+(m_{E}^{y})^{2}\right]\,, (11)

where mExm_{E}^{x} and mEym_{E}^{y} correspond to the two different components of the irreps, and are often refer as the ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} states [32, 31]. Previous works have shown that the states in the EE manifold are characterized by an accidental U(1) manifold spanned by the ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} states, resulting in the so-called Γ5\Gamma_{5} manifold [46, 20, 42].

Apart from the Γ5\Gamma_{5} manifold, which only considers the spin configurations spanned by the EE irrep, the degeneracy of the EE irrep with the A2A_{2} and the T1−T_{1-} irrep results in the emergence of additional accidental symmetries. To identify these manifolds, we consider a generic spin configuration in the ground-state manifold of the Hamiltonian along the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line parametrized by the six components comprising the three low-energy irreps44 4 The three low-energy degenerate irreps A2A_{2}, EE and T1−T_{1-} have different dimensions, being one-, two-, and three-dimensional, respectively, yielding a total of six degrees of freedom. constrained by Eq. (8). The constraint in Eq. (8) defines an S5S^{5} hypersphere of radius 2​S2S. Consequently, the spin configurations in the ground-state manifold described by this hypersphere are parametrized by five different angles (θ,ϕ,η,β,γ)(\theta,\phi,\eta,\beta,\gamma). In terms of these angles, the low-energy irrep components take the form

mA2=2​S​sin⁡θ​cos⁡ϕ,mEx=2​S​sin⁡θ​sin⁡ϕ​cos⁡η,mEy=2​S​sin⁡θ​sin⁡ϕ​sin⁡η,mT1−x=2​S​cos⁡θ​sin⁡β​cos⁡γ,mT1−y=2​S​cos⁡θ​sin⁡β​sin⁡γ,mT1−z=2​S​cos⁡θ​cos⁡β,\begin{split}&m_{A_{2}}=2S\sin{\theta}\cos{\phi},\\ &m_{E}^{x}=2S\sin{\theta}\sin{\phi}\cos{\eta},\\ &m_{E}^{y}=2S\sin{\theta}\sin{\phi}\sin{\eta},\\ &m_{T_{1-}}^{x}=2S\cos{\theta}\sin{\beta}\cos{\gamma},\\ &m_{T_{1-}}^{y}=2S\cos{\theta}\sin{\beta}\sin{\gamma},\\ &m_{T_{1-}}^{z}=2S\cos{\theta}\cos{\beta},\end{split} (12)

where θ\theta measures the mixing of T1−T_{1-} irrep with A2A_{2} and EE irreps, while the ϕ\phi angle quantifies the mixing between A2A_{2} and EE irreps, as introduced in Eq. (10). The angle η\eta specifies the ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} components of the EE irrep, while the T1−T_{1-} internal angles β\beta and γ\gamma characterize the T1−T_{1-} irrep orientation. The ground-state spin configurations defined by Eq. (12) are characterized by a tuple of five angles 𝝅=(θ,ϕ,η,β,γ)\bm{\pi}=(\theta,\phi,\eta,\beta,\gamma). However, these angles are strongly constrained by the local spin-length constraint in Eq. (7). For example, the spin-length constraint may be fulfilled by configurations with vanishing T1−T_{1-} contribution, where the angle θ\theta in Eq. (12) is fixed to θ=π/2\theta=\pi/2, and the angles ϕ\phi and η\eta are unconstrained. This particular choice of θ\theta defines a 2-sphere, which we refer to as the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere. The unconstrained character of the ϕ\phi and η\eta angles identifies two directions in which the spins can fluctuate with no energy cost, i.e., zero modes. These two zero modes are present in all the spin configurations in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere. Generic spin configurations in the ground-state manifold of the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line are expected to have a nonvanishing T1−T_{1-} contribution, i.e., without constraining the angle θ\theta. These can be constructed starting from a configuration in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere by applying a local rotation to the spins, which introduces a T1−T_{1-} contribution without violating the spin-length constraint. This implies that there are sets of angles ϕ\phi and η\eta from which an introduction of a nonvanishing T1−T_{1-} irrep fulfills the spin-length constraint. At these particular points, additional zero-modes away from the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere into a manifold of mixed states are associated with the spin configurations. To identify the set of points for which fluctuations into multiple degenerate manifolds are possible, we employ a gradient expansion of Eq. (7), yielding the four equations

δ​𝝅⋅∇(𝐒μ⋅𝐒μ)|𝝅0=0,\delta\bm{\pi}\cdot\left.\nabla(\mathbf{S}_{\mu}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{\mu})\right|_{\bm{\pi}_{0}}=0, (13)

to leading order in δ​𝝅=𝝅−𝝅0\delta\bm{\pi}=\bm{\pi}-\bm{\pi}_{0}, where 𝝅0\bm{\pi}_{0} is a ground-state spin configuration that satisfies the spin-length constraint, μ\mu is the sublattice index, and ∇=(∂θ,∂ϕ,∂η,∂β,∂γ)\nabla=(\partial_{\theta},\partial_{\phi},\partial_{\eta},\partial_{\beta},\partial_{\gamma}).

For more details on the derivation of the above equations, we refer the reader to Appendix B. For configurations in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere, Eq. (13) identifies three Jz±J_{z\pm}-dependent U(1) manifolds labeled as circles in Fig. 2. These three U(1) manifolds are parametrized by the equations

tanϕtanαmix=2cos⁡η+3​sin⁡η,tanϕtanαmix=2cos⁡η−3​sin⁡η,tanϕtanαmix=−1cos⁡η,\begin{split}\tan{\phi}\tan{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}&=\frac{2}{\cos{\eta}+\sqrt{3}\sin{\eta}},\\ \tan{\phi}\tan{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}&=\frac{2}{\cos{\eta}-\sqrt{3}\sin{\eta}},\\ \tan{\phi}\tan{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}&=-\frac{1}{\cos{\eta}},\end{split} (14)

where αmix\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}} is the splay angle defining the T1−T_{1-} irrep. We refer the reader to Appendix A for the definition of this quantity. For Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the three circles intersect at the poles of the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere. At these points, the spin configuration is described by a single irrep, namely the A2A_{2} irrep.55 5 This should not be surprising as for Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 both the EE and the T1−T_{1-} irreps modes have all spins lying in the local x​yxy. As such, the A2A_{2} mode, where the spins are aligned with the local zz direction, can smoothly fluctuate into all other states. As Jz±J_{z\pm} is varied, the three circles move away from the poles and closer to the equator where mA2=0m_{A_{2}}=0.

The presence of these additional zero-modes for the spin configurations defined by the U(1) manifolds shown in Fig. 2 plays a pivotal role in the entropy associated with these spin configurations. Spin configurations with these additional zero-modes are typically associated with higher entropy compared to other energetically degenerate configurations. In the next sections, we study the impact of these additional zero-modes on the low-temperature thermal selection of a spin configuration in the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line.

III Classical Low-Temperature Expansion

Classical low-temperature expansion is a method that analyzes the thermal spin fluctuation about a classical ground-state configuration [23]. At low temperatures, the spins are mostly polarized along a (local) ordering direction with small perpendicular fluctuations δ​niα¯\delta n_{i}^{\bar{\alpha}}. In this low-temperature limit, the spin configurations may be approximated by

𝐒i≃(δ​nix~,δ​niy~,S⁡(1−(δ​nix~)22​S2−(δ​niy~)2​S2)),\mathbf{S}_{i}\simeq\left(\delta n_{i}^{\tilde{x}},\delta n_{i}^{\tilde{y}},S\left(1-\frac{(\delta n_{i}^{\tilde{x}})^{2}}{2S^{2}}-\frac{(\delta n_{i}^{\tilde{y}})}{2S^{2}}\right)\right)\,, (15)

where the coordinate system is chosen such that the z~\tilde{z} axis aligns with the ii-site ground-state spin, and δ​nα~≪1\delta n^{\tilde{\alpha}}\ll 1. For a particular ground-state configuration 𝝅0\bm{\pi}_{0}, applying the ansatz in Eq. (15) to the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) allows us to obtain a low-temperature effective Hamiltonian governing spin fluctuations δ​nα~\delta n^{\tilde{\alpha}} about the spin state 𝝅0\bm{\pi}_{0}. This approximation results in a single-tetrahedron effective Hamiltonian where the spins interact via the 8×88\times 8 Hessian matrix ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2}. In terms of ℋ2\mathcal{H}_{2}, the low-temperature free energy of a spin configuration in the ground-state manifold yields

ℱ\displaystyle\mathcal{F} =ℋ0−T​𝒮\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{0}-T\mathcal{S}
=ℋ0−T⁡(N​ln⁡T−12​∑𝐪ln⁡det​ℋ2​(𝐪)),\displaystyle=\mathcal{H}_{0}-T\left(N\ln{T}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mathbf{q}}\ln{\operatorname{det}\mathcal{H}_{2}(\mathbf{q})}\right), (16)

where ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0} is the classical ground-state energy, 𝒮\mathcal{S} corresponds to the entropy resulting from thermal spin fluctuations, and ℋ2​(𝐪)\mathcal{H}_{2}(\mathbf{q}) represents the Hessian matrix in reciprocal space. Equation (16) is used to compute the entropy associated with different spin configurations with the same classical ground-state energy ℋ0\mathcal{H}_{0}. In this approximation, the state with the highest associated entropy is expected to be thermally favored at low temperatures.

III.1 Entropy in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere as a function of Jz±J_{z\pm}

We study the entropy associated with the states in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere via a classical low-temperature expansion, and study its dependence as a function of Jz±J_{z\pm}. Figure 3(a)-(i) illustrates a stereographic projection of the entropy (modulo a Jz±J_{z\pm} and TT dependent constant) for the states in the upper half of the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere and along a one-dimensional cut of the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere for η=0\eta=0. Both the stereographic projections and the cuts are illustrated for four distinct values of Jz±J_{z\pm}. In this figure, the entropy obtained via the classical low-temperature expansion exposes three circular trajectories, where the entropy is higher, corresponding to the U(1) manifolds shown in Fig. 2. For Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the spin configuration with the highest entropy is obtained for the A2A_{2} configuration, corresponding to the point where the three U(1) manifolds intersect, see Fig. 3(a) and (b). Furthermore, we note that, at Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the ℋ2​(𝒒)\mathcal{H}_{2}(\bm{q}) matrix in Eq. (16) presents two zero-energy flat bands.66 6 This implies that there are two spin fluctuation modes about the A2A_{2} configuration which are not quadratic. As Jz±J_{z\pm} is varied, the U(1) manifolds drift away from the A2A_{2} configuration. It is worth noting that, for Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0, the entropy reaches its maximum value at states where η=2​π​n/3\eta=2\pi n/3 with n∈{0,1,2}n\in\{0,1,2\}, i.e., states for which the contribution of the EE irrep to the ground-state configuration is solely described by a ψ2\psi_{2} configuration. The one-dimensional cuts along η=0\eta=0 for distinct values of Jz±J_{z\pm} reveal how the maximal entropy, and therefore minimal free energy, takes place at two possible values, which we label ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2}. The value of ϕ1\phi_{1} is obtained at points where the U(1) manifolds defined by Eq. (14) intersect. These intersections occur at six points in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere defined by the constraints

tanϕtanαmix=2atη=0,2​π3,4​π3,tanϕtanαmix=−2atη=π3,π,5​π3,\begin{split}\tan\phi\tan\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}=2\quad\mathrm{at}\quad\eta=0,\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3},\\ \tan\phi\tan\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}=-2\quad\mathrm{at}\quad\eta=\frac{\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{5\pi}{3},\end{split} (17)

indicated by the red stars in Fig. 3(j). On the other hand, for Jz±J_{z\pm} slightly below the boundary Jz±=2J_{z\pm}=\sqrt{2} of the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line, the six states with the highest entropy are now defined by the angle ϕ2\phi_{2} which is defined by the constraints

tanϕtanαmix=−1atη=0,2​π3,4​π3tanϕtanαmix=1atη=π3,π,5​π3\begin{split}\tan\phi\tan\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}=-1\quad\mathrm{at}\quad\eta=0,\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{4\pi}{3}\\ \tan\phi\tan\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}=1\quad\mathrm{at}\quad\eta=\frac{\pi}{3},\pi,\frac{5\pi}{3}\end{split} (18)

that also live on the U(1) manifolds defined by Eq. (14), as marked by the light blue squares in Fig. 3(j). A detailed study of the entropy as a function of Jz±J_{z\pm} along the η=0\eta=0 line identifies two high-entropy states which smoothly evolve from the A2A_{2} state at Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0 to two mixed states at nonzero Jz±J_{z\pm}, see the high-intensity lines in Fig. 3(k). These states correspond to the Jz±J_{z\pm}-dependent angles ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2}.

According to our classical low-temperature expansion study of the entropy, the maximal-entropy configuration swaps from (η,ϕ)=(0,ϕ1)(\eta,\phi)=(0,\phi_{1}) to (η,ϕ)=(0,ϕ2)(\eta,\phi)=(0,\phi_{2}) at the value Jz±⋆≃1.26J_{z\pm}^{\star}\simeq 1.26. For values of Jz±J_{z\pm} in the close proximity to Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star}, the states defined by the combined triangle-shaped segments of the U(1) manifolds around the north pole feature an approximately equal entropy. We refer to Appendix D for further discussion regarding the classical low-temperature expansion and the definition of Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star}.

IV Landau theory

In this section, we construct a minimal Landau theory and provide further insights on the possible 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases, the transitions between them, and the evolution of the order parameters mIm_{I}. Given that our Monte Carlo simulations identify contributions from only the A2A_{2} and EE irreps to the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases (see Sec. V), we construct a Landau theory based on these two order parameters.77 7 This approximation is further motivated by the fact that the only terms in the Landau free-energy theory which mix the 𝐦T1−\mathbf{m}_{T_{1-}} order parameter with the remaining order parameters are fully already invariant under the tetrahedral symmetry group TdT_{d}. Following Ref. [51], we consider the local magnetic order parameters defined as

mEx\displaystyle m_{E}^{x} =14​N​∑iSix,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{i}S^{x}_{i}, mEy\displaystyle m_{E}^{y} =14​N​∑iSiy,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{i}S^{y}_{i}, mA2\displaystyle m_{A_{2}} =14​N​∑iSiz,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{4N}\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}, (19)

where mExm_{E}^{x}, mEym_{E}^{y}, and mA2m_{A_{2}} measure the local xx, yy, and zz magnetic moment, respectively, and correspond to global order parameters associated with the components of the EE and A2A_{2} irreps. It is useful to introduce the complex order parameter

mx​y=|𝐦E|​ei​η,\displaystyle m_{xy}=|\mathbf{m}_{E}|e^{i\eta}, (20)

which measures the local x​yxy magnetic moment, where the angle η\eta indicates the direction of the magnetic moment in the local x​yxy planes, whereas the magnitude of the complex parameter agrees with that of the EE order parameter, i.e. |mx​y|=|𝐦E||m_{xy}|=|\mathbf{m}_{E}|. We construct the Landau theory by considering the action of the group TdT_{d} over the local magnetic moments. It is worth noting that the C3C_{3} symmetry around local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle direction constraints the terms of the form mx​yk+(mx​y∗)k=2​|𝐦E|k​cos⁡k​ηm_{xy}^{k}+(m_{xy}^{\ast})^{k}=2|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{k}\cos k\eta to those for which k∈3​ℤk\in 3\mathbb{Z}. For an extensive discussion of all symmetry-allowed terms up to the sixth order, we refer the reader to Appendix E. Here, we consider the minimal Landau theory of the form

ℱminimal=ℱ0+r0​|𝐦E|2+r1​mA22+r2​|𝐦E|4+rx​y​z​mA22​|𝐦E|2+r3​mA24+r4​|𝐦E|6+ω​mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η+f6​|𝐦E|6​cos⁡6​η+ℱ⁡[𝐦T1−]+𝒪⁡[mI8]\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_{\mathrm{minimal}}&=\mathcal{F}_{0}+r_{0}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2}+r_{1}m_{A_{2}}^{2}+r_{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{4}+r_{xyz}m_{A_{2}}^{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2}\\ &+r_{3}m_{A_{2}}^{4}+r_{4}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{6}+\omega m_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta}\\ &+f_{6}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{6}\cos{6\eta}+\mathcal{F}[\mathbf{m}_{T_{1-}}]+\mathcal{O}[m_{I}^{8}]\end{split} (21)

which resembles the Landau theory provided by Ref. [51], with the additional terms parameterized by rx​y​zr_{xyz} and r3r_{3}. In the above, ℱ⁡[𝐦T1−]\mathcal{F}[\mathbf{m}_{T_{1-}}] corresponds to terms in the Landau theory which possess a T1−T_{1-} dependence. In the following analysis, we set these to zero as this particular magnetic order is not observed in our Monte Carlo results discussed in Sec. V.88 8 We note that this simplification implies that this Landau theory can also be used to characterize models describing the phase boundary between the A2A_{2} and EE irreps. For a given set of parameters {r0,r1,r2,rx​y​z,r3,ω,f6}\{r_{0},r_{1},r_{2},r_{xyz},r_{3},\omega,f_{6}\}, we find the solution with the lowest free energy numerically.

Figure 4 shows the mean-field phase diagram and the evolution of the magnetic order parameters as a function of the tuning parameters r0r_{0} and r1r_{1}, for fixed values of the remaining parameters. From the evolution of the order parameters, we identify three distinct phases; a paramagnetic phase, where |mA2|=0|m_{A_{2}}|=0 and |𝐦E|=0|\mathbf{m}_{E}|=0, an A2A_{2} phase, where |mA2|≠0|m_{A_{2}}|\neq 0 and |𝐦E|=0|\mathbf{m}_{E}|=0, and a mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, where |mA2|≠0|m_{A_{2}}|\neq 0 and |𝐦E|≠0|\mathbf{m}_{E}|\neq 0. Importantly, we find that η=n​π3\eta=\frac{n\pi}{3} with n∈{0,1,2,3,4,5}n\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5\} in the mixed phase, corresponding to an A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} state.

The color plots shown in Figs. 4(a) and (b) suggest continuous phase transitions from the paramagnetic phase to the ordered phases A2A_{2} and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2}, and first-order transition between the A2A_{2} and the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phases. To more clearly expose the nature of the transitions obtained within Landau theory, we illustrate in Fig. 4(c)-(f) line cuts illustrating the evolution of the order parameters as a phase boundary is crossed. These line cuts are marked in Figs. 4(a) and (b) by dashed green paths. Figure 4(c) illustrates the evolution of the order parameters in the line cut between points marked 1 and 2 in Figure 4(a) and (b) in the paramagnetic and A2A_{2} phases, respectively. Along this line, the mA2m_{A_{2}} order parameter shows a square-root-like behavior, while |𝐦E|=0|\mathbf{m}_{E}|=0. On the other hand, for the line cut between points 1 and 3, corresponding to points in the paramagnetic and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, respectively, both order parameters become nonzero as soon as the phase boundary is crossed. It is worth noting that the A2A_{2} order parameter remains small compared to the EE order parameter in the vicinity of the phase boundary and for larger values of r1r_{1}, see Fig. 4(b). The continuous evolution of the parameter across these two phase boundaries indicate a continuous phase transition between the paramagnetic phase and the ordered phases. Lastly, Figs. 4(e) and (f) illustrate the evolution of the order parameters for the line cut between points 2 and 4 corresponding to points in the A2A_{2} phase and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase for two distinct sets of (r2,rx​y​z,r3,r4,ω,f6)(r_{2},r_{xyz},r_{3},r_{4},\omega,f_{6}) parameters. In both cases, we observe how the EE order parameter presents a large finite jump when crossing into the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, while the A2A_{2} order parameter presents a small jump. The size of the small discontinuous jump in the A2A_{2} parameter and its evolution in the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase are parameter dependent, as seen when comparing Figs. 4(e) and (f). The discontinuous nature of the order parameters, which is more drastically evidenced in the EE order parameter, indicates that these two phases are separated by a first-order phase transition.

V Classical Monte Carlo simulations

In this section, we present numerical Monte Carlo simulations used to obtain the finite-temperature phase diagram shown in Fig. 1. A wide range of temperatures is considered for several values of Jz±J_{z\pm} on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line. Our simulations expose a rich phase diagram with a variety of symmetry-breaking phases being realized. In particular, we find two 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 long-range ordered phases, namely the A2A_{2} and the mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phases, which are defined at the level of a single tetrahedron. We reiterate that ψ2\psi_{2} corresponds to the xx component of the EE irrep. Furthermore, we find a spin nematic phase that is stabilized at low and intermediate temperatures around the point Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2}, where the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) acquires additional subsystem symmetries. At Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2}, these additional symmetries prevent any type of conventional magnetic order, resulting in the stabilization of the spin nematic phase down to the lowest temperatures. The spin nematic phase is characterized by broken cubic spin rotational symmetry, but unbroken time reversal symmetry.

The section is organized as follows. First, we introduce algorithmic details and the measured observables in Secs. V.1 and V.2, respectively. Our results for the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases are shown in Sec. V.3. We also compare the Monte Carlo results with the predictions from classical low-temperature expansion and Landau theory. The spin nematic phase stemming from the zero temperature Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} point deserves its own discussion as it presents several additional features. We postpone its discussion to Sec. VI.

V.1 Algorithmic details

We study the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) using large-scale classical Monte Carlo simulations. We employ Metropolis [52] and over-relaxation algorithms [53] combined with parallel tempering exchange [54, 55, 56]. The spins are treated as classical vectors of unit length 𝐒i2=1\mathbf{S}_{i}^{2}=1. Each lattice sweep of a Metropolis update is combined with 20 over-relaxation steps followed by a replica exchange trial of the configurations at adjacent temperatures. To decorrelate measures, the procedure is repeated 20 times between two consecutive measurements on the lattice. We consider pyrochlore lattices with L3L^{3} tetrahedra and N=4​L3N=4L^{3} sites, using L=6,8,10,12L=6,8,10,12 with periodic boundary conditions. The accumulated statistics are of the order 𝒪⁡(105)\mathcal{O}(10^{5}) for each point in parameter space. The simulations are carried out on the high-performance computer Barnard at the NHR Center of TU Dresden [57].

V.2 Observables

We measure the following thermodynamic observables in the simulations:

Specific heat.

From energy fluctuations, we measure the specific heat as

C≔1N​T2​(⟨ℋ2⟩−⟨ℋ⟩2),C\coloneqq\frac{1}{NT^{2}}({\langle\mathcal{H}^{2}\rangle-\langle\mathcal{H}\rangle^{2}}), (22)

with TT the absolute temperature and NN the total number of sites.

Magnetic order parameters.

Magnetic order parameters are constructed on the single-tetrahedron irreps 𝐦I\mathbf{m}_{I}, I=A2,E,T2,T1±I=A_{2},E,T_{2},T_{1\pm} as

⟨mI⟩=⟨|12​S​L3​∑⊠𝐦I⊠|⟩,\langle m_{I}\rangle=\left\langle\left|\frac{1}{2SL^{3}}\sum_{\boxtimes}\mathbf{m}_{I}^{\boxtimes}\right|\right\rangle, (23)

where ∑⊠\sum_{\boxtimes} denotes the sum over all tetrahedra on the lattice and 𝐦I⊠\mathbf{m}_{I}^{\boxtimes} corresponds to the II-th irrep mode in the ⊠\boxtimes tetrahedron. The single-tetrahedron irreps modes are expressed in terms of the spin components, as reported in the Table 2 of Appendix A. The observables in Eq. (23) are normalized such that ∑I⟨mI⟩2=1\sum_{I}\langle m_{I}\rangle^{2}=1 in the low-temperature limit.

Sublattice magnetic order parameter.

The sublattice magnetic order parameter provides a measure of whether any form of magnetic long-range order develops on the individual sublattices and is defined as

⟨msub2⟩=⟨14​∑μ|12​S​L3​∑⊠𝐒⊠,μ|2⟩,\langle m^{2}_{\mathrm{sub}}\rangle=\left\langle\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\mu}\left|\frac{1}{2SL^{3}}\sum_{\boxtimes}\mathbf{S}_{\boxtimes,\mu}\right|^{2}\right\rangle\,, (24)

where μ\mu denotes the sublattice index in the tetrahedron ⊠\boxtimes, and 𝐒⊠,μ\mathbf{S}_{\boxtimes,\mu} is the corresponding spin vector.

Magnetic susceptibilities.

We also measure the susceptibilities of the magnetic order parameters,

χI=NT(⟨mI2⟩−⟨mI⟩2),I=A2,E,T2,T1±.\displaystyle\chi_{I}=\frac{N}{T}(\langle m_{I}^{2}\rangle-\langle m_{I}\rangle^{2}),\qquad I=A_{2},E,T_{2},T_{1\pm}. (25)
Binder cumulants.

To extract the location of the transition points from the finite-size simulations and to analyze the natures of the transition, it is also useful to measure renormalization-group-invariant Binder cumulants defined as

UI=⟨mI4⟩⟨mI2⟩2,I=A2,E,T2,T1±.\displaystyle U_{I}=\frac{\langle m_{I}^{4}\rangle}{\langle m_{I}^{2}\rangle^{2}},\qquad I=A_{2},E,T_{2},T_{1\pm}. (26)
EE irrep order parameter.

In order to distinguish between the ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} components of the EE irrep in the case of EE long-range order, we also measure the so-called ⟨mE​6⟩\langle m_{E6}\rangle parameter, defined as

⟨mE​6⟩=⟨mE​cos⁡6​η⟩,\langle m_{E6}\rangle=\left\langle m_{E}\cos 6\eta\right\rangle, (27)

where η\eta quantifies the angle of the spin configurations in the EE manifold [58, 23, 59], see Eq. 12. It reduces to η=n​π/3\eta=n\pi/3 if the ψ2\psi_{2} component is realized, while it assumes the values η=(2​n+1)​π/6\eta=(2n+1)\pi/6 when the ψ3\psi_{3} component is achieved, with n∈ℤn\in\mathbb{Z} in both cases. Consequently, the ⟨mE​6⟩\langle m_{E6}\rangle parameter acquires a positive (negative) value when the spin configurations in the low-temperature phase are described by a ψ2\psi_{2} (ψ3\psi_{3}) configuration.

Spin-nematic order parameter.

The single-site spin-nematic order parameter is a five-component vector [60, 61, 62, 11, 63, 64] obtained by combining the five symmetric traceless 3×33\times 3 matrices Λ(α)\Lambda^{(\alpha)},

Λ(α)={13(−1000−10002),(−100010000),(000001010),(001000100),(010100000)},\begin{split}\Lambda^{(\alpha)}=\Biggl\{\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}&\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 0&-1&0\\ 0&0&2\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\ 0&1&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0&0&0\\ 0&0&1\\ 0&1&0\end{pmatrix},\\ &\begin{pmatrix}0&0&1\\ 0&0&0\\ 1&0&0\end{pmatrix},\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\ 1&0&0\\ 0&0&0\end{pmatrix}\Biggl\},\end{split} (28)

with the traceless symmetric tensor 𝖰iμ​ν=Siμ​Siν−13​δμ​ν\mathsf{Q}^{\mu\nu}_{i}=S^{\mu}_{i}S^{\nu}_{i}-\frac{1}{3}\delta^{\mu\nu}, as

diα=32​Tr⁡[𝖰i​Λ(α)],d^{\alpha}_{i}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\operatorname{Tr}[\mathsf{Q}_{i}\Lambda^{(\alpha)}]\,, (29)

where the normalization factor is fixed by demanding a unitary absolute value of 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} if any a nematic state is realized. Explicitly, the five components of 𝐝i\mathbf{d}_{i} read

di1=12​[2​(Siz)2−(Six)2−(Siy)2],di2=−32​[(Six)2−(Siy)2],di3=3SixSiy,di4=3SixSiz,di5=3SiySiz.\begin{split}d^{1}_{i}&=\frac{1}{2}\left[2(S_{i}^{z})^{2}-(S_{i}^{x})^{2}-(S_{i}^{y})^{2}\right]\,,\\ d^{2}_{i}&=-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\left[(S_{i}^{x})^{2}-(S_{i}^{y})^{2}\right]\,,\\ d_{i}^{3}&=\sqrt{3}S_{i}^{x}S_{i}^{y}\,,\quad d_{i}^{4}=\sqrt{3}S_{i}^{x}S_{i}^{z}\,,\quad d_{i}^{5}=\sqrt{3}S_{i}^{y}S_{i}^{z}\,.\end{split}

In the Monte Carlo simulations, we measure the long-range spin-nematic order parameter as

⟨mnem⟩=⟨|14​S2​L3​∑i𝐝i|⟩.\langle m_{\mathrm{nem}}\rangle=\left<\left|\frac{1}{4S^{2}L^{3}}\sum_{i}\mathbf{d}_{i}\right|\right>\,. (30)

By construction, this order parameter is also nonzero in the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 ordered phases we observe.99 9 For example, for an A2A_{2} state, we obtain 𝐝=(1,0,0,0,0)\mathbf{d}=(1,0,0,0,0). However, in the regions where the ordinary long-range irreps order parameters in Eq. (23) vanish, the quantity in Eq. (30) can still be finite, signaling a spin-nematic phase with unbroken time-reversal symmetry and broken spin rotational symmetry.

Static spin structure factor.

The static spin structure factor is defined as

S(𝐪)=1N∑i,j⟨𝐒i⋅𝐒j⟩e−i𝐪⋅(𝐑i−𝐑j),S({\mathbf{q}})=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i,j}\langle\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{j}\rangle\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{R}_{i}-\mathbf{R}_{j})}, (31)

where 𝐑i\mathbf{R}_{i} is the position vector of the site ii on the lattice.

V.3 Magnetic q = 0 phases

In the following, we present the numerical results from Monte Carlo simulations. First, the non-Kramers case is covered, then the finite Jz±J_{z\pm} Kramers results are reported.

V.3.1 Non-Kramers case Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0

At Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) describes a non-Kramers spin system, where the local zz components of pseudospins transform as magnetic dipoles and the local x​yxy components transform as magnetic quadrupoles [5, 65]. In this case, the T1−T_{1-} irrep mode corresponds to a splayed ferromagnet where the spins lie on the local x​yxy planes of each sublattice, see Appendix A for details. Consequently, both the EE and the T1−T_{1-} irreps are regarded as local x​yxy irreps, with the spin configurations for these irreps lying on the local x​yxy planes, while the A2A_{2} irrep is a local zz irrep. For Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the Monte Carlo data indicate a phase transition from a paramagnetic phase into an A2A_{2} long-range-ordered phase at Tc=0.957​(1)T_{\mathrm{c}}=0.957(1). The A2A_{2} long-range order extends down to the lowest temperatures we considered and agrees with the predictions from the classical low-temperature expansion discussed in Sec. III, see Fig. 5. The A2A_{2} irreps transform as a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} object, so the critical behavior is expected to fall in the three-dimensional Ising universality class, at least asymptotically, if the transition is continuous. Finite-size scaling allows us to extract the exponent ν=0.635​(8)\nu=0.635(8) and γ=1.205​(15)\gamma=1.205(15), consistent with the three-dimensional Ising universality class [66, 67].

As the temperature approaches zero, the specific heat does not reach a unitary value, as expected from the equipartition theorem for purely quadratic fluctuations, implying that the low-energy fluctuations about the ground-state configuration are of higher order [68, 17, 30]. Indeed, as we already briefly mentioned in Sec. III, the classical low-temperature expansion finds that the matrix ℋ2​(𝐪)\mathcal{H}_{2}(\mathbf{q}) has two zero-energy flat bands in momentum space, meaning that two out of the eight fluctuation modes are not captured by the quadratic approximation, therefore identifying two of these fluctuation modes as quartic or higher modes. In the case the fluctuations modes are only quadratic and quartic in nature, the specific heat in the low-temperature limit is expected to asymptotically approach the value

CkB=14​(n22+n44)\frac{C}{k_{\rm B}}=\frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{n_{2}}{2}+\frac{n_{4}}{4}\right) (32)

where n2n_{2} is the number of quadratic modes and n4n_{4} is the number of quartic modes, and n2+n4=8n_{2}+n_{4}=8 is the total number of fluctuation modes. Under the assumption that the two zero modes obtained in the second-order classical low-temperature expansion evolve into quartic modes when higher-order fluctuations are considered, corresponding to n2=6n_{2}=6 and n4=2n_{4}=2, the predicted low-temperature specific heat is CkB=7/8\frac{C}{k_{\mathrm{B}}}=7/8. As illustrated in Fig. 5(a), this value is asymptotically approached by the specific heat in the low-temperature regime, validating the quartic-modes hypothesis.

V.3.2 Kramers case Jz±≠0J_{z\pm}\neq 0

In contrast to the non-Kramers system, all the spin components in a Kramers system transform as magnetic dipoles, allowing for a nonvanishing Jz±J_{z\pm} coupling. In this case, the classical low-temperature expansion identifies mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} states as the maximal entropy spin configurations, see Fig. 3(k). Our Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the low-temperature state along the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line realizes a mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, where the order parameters associated to these two magnetic orders acquire finite values in the low-temperature regime, with the exception of the immediate vicinity of the point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}. Our low-temperature Monte Carlo simulations in fact show a remarkable quantitative agreement with the classical low-temperature expansion predictions at low temperatures (see Sec. III). The qualitative features associated with the transitions and order parameter evolutions are well captured by the Landau theory (see Sec. IV). A detailed comparison is provided at the end of this section. For the low-temperature regime, it is crucial to highlight that the predictions of the classical low-temperature expansion are only valid in this low-temperature region of the phase diagram. Indeed, and as elucidated in recent works [41, 37, 58], the state selected at high temperatures can differ from those selected at intermediate and low temperatures. Indeed, our Monte Carlo simulations reveal a more intricate phase diagram, characterized by a cascade of phase transitions between the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases and the nematic phase, which are not exposed by the classical low-temperature expansion. Ultimately, the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase is approached in different ways as temperature is lowered, depending on the value of Jz±J_{z\pm}. It is worth noting that, in our Monte Carlo simulations, the long-range A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E order is well captured by the long-range order parameters in Eq. (23). These parameters, however, are not able to differentiate between ψ2\psi_{2} and ψ3\psi_{3} components of the EE irreps. For this purpose, we have also studied the evolution of the so-called ⟨mE​6⟩\langle m_{E6}\rangle parameter, see Appendix F. In what follows, we discuss the results obtained for the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases in two parameter regimes, one for a small coupling Jz±≲1/2J_{z\pm}\lesssim 1/\sqrt{2} and one for a large coupling Jz±≳1/2J_{z\pm}\gtrsim 1/\sqrt{2}.

Small coupling Jz±≲0.5J_{z\pm}\lesssim 0.5.

For sufficiently small Jz±J_{z\pm}, the low-temperature phase is reached through two phase transitions located at Tc1T_{\mathrm{c}1} and Tc2T_{\mathrm{c}2}, with Tc1<Tc2T_{\mathrm{c}1}<T_{\mathrm{c}2}, see Fig. 1. The higher-temperature transition at Tc2T_{\mathrm{c}2} is continuous and takes the system from the paramagnetic phase to an A2A_{2} ordered phase. The lower-temperature transition is discontinuous and takes the system from the A2A_{2} order phase to the mixed A2⊗ψ2A_{2}\otimes\psi_{2} phase.

Figure 6 illustrates a representative example of the specific heat, order parameters, and irrep-magnitude distribution for Jz±=0.4J_{z\pm}=0.4. The specific heat depicted in Fig. 6(a) develops two sharp features at Tc​1T_{c1} and Tc​2T_{c2}, signaling the phase transitions. We note that the peak at Tc​2T_{c2} slowly increases with system size, indicating a continuous transition with a small α/ν\alpha/\nu critical-exponent ratio. In this temperature regime, the mA2m_{A_{2}} order parameter varies smoothly, see Fig. 6(b) with a diverging slope at the transition, similar to the behavior seen in the Landau theory. Finite-size scaling of the respective Binder parameter around Tc2T_{\mathrm{c}2} yields a value of the correlation-length exponent ν=0.63​(2)\nu=0.63(2), in well agreement with the theoretical value ν=0.62997\nu=0.62997 for the three-dimensional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} universality class. However, the finite-size scaling on the susceptibility χA2\chi_{A_{2}} yields a ratio γ/ν=1.66​(4)\gamma/\nu=1.66(4) which is quite far from the expected value γ/ν=1.9637\gamma/\nu=1.9637 for the three-dimensional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} universality class [66, 67]. This disagreement may be caused a slow renormalization group flow in our microscopic model on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line, leading to sizable finite-size corrections to the asymptotically expected critical behavior [22, 66].1010 10 Although possibly slightly more pronounced in our case, similar deviations from the respective expected universality were also observed in the context of Heisenberg-Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya pyrochlores [22].

As the system cools down, our Monte Carlo simulations detect a rapid change at T=Tc1T=T_{\mathrm{c}1} in the A2{A_{2}} and EE order parameters, shown in Figs. 6(b) and (c). This jump, in addition to the sharp peak of the specific heat, shown in Fig. 6(a), allows us to identify this transition as a first-order transition. In the low-temperature phase, the EE order parameter ⟨mE⟩\langle m_{E}\rangle jumps to a finite value, effectively reducing the magnitude of ⟨mA2⟩\langle m_{A_{2}}\rangle.

The phase transitions and their nature can be interpreted in the following way. The relevant symmetries are represented by time reversal symmetry Θ\Theta and three-fold rotation symmetry C3C_{3}, which are isomorphic to a ℤ2⊗ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{2}\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{3} symmetry group structure. Time reversal (ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2}) symmetry breaking is spontaneously broken at Tc2T_{\mathrm{c}2} with the possibility of a continuous transition in the three-dimensional Ising universality class, which seems to be numerically realized. The residual rotational C3C_{3} symmetry (ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3}) is broken at Tc1T_{\mathrm{c}1}, realizing a first-order phase transition as expected from three-state clock models or three-state Potts model [69].

To further characterize the low-temperature mixed phase observed below Tc​1T_{c1}, we employ Eq. (10) to extract the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} mixing angle ϕ\phi. The mixing angle between these irreps is obtained by measuring the distribution of the magnitude of the local single-tetrahedron irreps, i.e., the distribution obtained from the magnitude of the irreps in the L3L^{3} tetrahedra in a single full-system configuration [15, 30] [see Fig. 6(d) for the coordinate frame used for these distributions]. Since the T1−T_{1-} irrep is strongly thermally depopulated at temperatures below Tc​1T_{c1}, the distribution of the single-tetrahedron irreps lies close to the equator line of the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E mixed phase, with θ≈π/2\theta\approx\pi/2. This is illustrated in the histogram of the single-tetrahedron irreps shown in Fig. 6(e). Below Tc1T_{c_{1}}, the distribution is concentrated around a finite value of ϕ\phi, which effectively quantifies the mixing between the A2A_{2} and EE irreps, see the white dashed line in Fig. 6(e). The precise location at which the distribution concentrates at low temperatures depends on Jz±J_{z\pm}, implying that the mixing angle ϕ\phi defining the low-temperature phase drifts as a function of Jz±J_{z\pm}, in agreement with the results of the classical low-temperature expansion.

Large coupling Jz±≳0.9J_{z\pm}\gtrsim 0.9.

For sufficiently large Jz±J_{z\pm}, approximately Jz±≳0.9J_{z\pm}\gtrsim 0.9, the low-temperature A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase is reached through a single continuous phase transition at critical TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, see Fig. 1. Figure 7 illustrates a representative example of the specific heat and irrep order parameters for Jz±=1.2J_{z\pm}=1.2. In this large-coupling regime, the specific heat peaks at TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, followed by a broad hump at lower temperatures, see Fig. 7(a). Reducing the temperature below TcT_{\mathrm{c}}, ⟨mE⟩\langle m_{E}\rangle continuously increases to a moderate value, while ⟨mA2⟩\langle{m}_{A_{2}}\rangle initially increases only very slowly, see Figs. 7(b) and (c). As the system is cooled below temperatures where the hump in the specific heat is observed, ⟨mA2⟩\langle{m}_{A_{2}}\rangle starts to also increase significantly. Concurrently, the ⟨mE⟩\langle m_{E}\rangle keeps on increasing as the system is further cooled, with only minor changes in the slope of this order parameter.

Given that the ψ2\psi_{2} and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} spin configurations break the same symmetries, the low-temperature hump in the specific heat should be interpreted as a crossover from a region with dominant ψ2\psi_{2} order to one with moderate order in both the A2A_{2} and ψ\psi irreps, rather than as a genuine phase transition.1111 11 Here we have excluded the possibility of a first-order phase transition, as the finite-size scaling of the hump in the specific heat does not indicate a linear dependence of this feature with LL. This interpretation is further supported by the behavior of the A2A_{2} Binder cumulant and susceptibility. The Binder cumulant shows no crossing point, as would be expected for a genuine phase transition, and the susceptibility exhibits no divergence with increasing system size (see Appendix F). Given that the internal energies of the ψ2\psi_{2} and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} spin configurations are degenerate by construction, the low-temperature hump in the specific heat reflects the entropy release associated with thermal fluctuations of the A2A_{2} irrep, while all symmetry breaking occurs at TcT_{\mathrm{c}}.

The precise location of TcT_{\mathrm{c}} is determined from the EE Binder cumulant, showing a common crossing point at different sizes at the critical temperature. We also attempted to characterize the critical behavior by extracting critical indices from the finite-size scaling of the Binder cumulant and the EE susceptibility, obtaining ν=0.65​(2)\nu=0.65(2) and γ/ν=1.60​(2)\gamma/\nu=1.60(2). The transition and its nature can be interpreted within the following scenario. The symmetry group ℤ2⊗ℤ3≈ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{2}\otimes\mathbb{Z}_{3}\approx\mathbb{Z}_{6} is spontaneously broken, both ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} and ℤ3\mathbb{Z}_{3}, at TcT_{\mathrm{c}}. At criticality, the ℤ6\mathbb{Z}_{6} anisotropies are irrelevant and the system experiences a symmetry enlargement to the continuous U(1) group [70], so the critical behavior could fall, at least asymptotically, into the three-dimensional U(1) universality class, characterized by ν=0.6717\nu=0.6717 and γ/ν=1.9618\gamma/\nu=1.9618 [66, 71, 72]. Comparing the finite-size scaling critical exponents with those of the three-dimensional U(1) universality class, we find that ν\nu agrees with the theoretical value within error bars, whereas γ/ν\gamma/\nu deviates significantly. A possible explanation is a slow renormalization-group flow in our microscopic model along the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line, similar to the case for small Jz±J_{z\pm} discussed in the previous paragraph (see also Ref. [22]).

Comparison with predictions from classical low-temperature expansion and Landau theory.

Except in the immediate vicinity of the point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}, our Monte Carlo simulations reveal a mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} low-temperature ground state throughout the phase diagram, in agreement with the expectation from the classical low-temperature expansion (see Sec. III). In fact, the agreement with the classical low-temperature expansion expectations can be assessed on a quantitative level by studying the single-tetrahedron-irrep-magnitude distribution on the full lattice configurations obtained from Monte Carlo simulations, and measuring the resulting mixing angles in the low-temperature regime, see, e.g., the irrep-magnitude distribution on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} manifold shown in Fig. 6(e). From the distributions, we extract the average A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E mixing angle ϕ\phi, which may be compared with the corresponding expectation from the classical low-temperature expansion, see, e.g., Fig. 3.1212 12 Since we measured the magnitude of the irreps in the classical Monte Carlo simulations, the corresponding mixing angle is restricted to ϕ∈[0,π/2]\phi\in[0,\pi/2]. This means that mixing angles ϕ>π/2\phi>\pi/2 obtained in the classical low-temperature expansion need to be reflected as ϕ→π−ϕ\phi\rightarrow\pi-\phi to facilitate comparison with the corresponding angles measured in the Monte Carlo simulations. Figure 8 shows, within error bars, excellent agreement between classical Monte Carlo simulations and the classical low-temperature expansion across the entire phase diagram, thereby linking the low-temperature order-by-disorder phenomenon discussed in Sec. III to the corresponding regions of the quasi-exact Monte Carlo phase diagram. In particular, the angle extracted from the Monte Carlo data also presents a jump around the position Jz±⋆≈1.26J_{z\pm}^{\star}\approx 1.26 predicted from the classical low-temperature expansion. It is caused by the change in the highest-entropy configuration described by the two A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} branches, see Sec. III, and can be interpreted as an unnecessary first-order transition within the same phase, tuned by Jz±J_{z\pm} at fixed temperature, between two A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} configurations with different mixing angles ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2}.1313 13 Up to our maximal sizes, we cannot resolve this transition in the specific heat, while it is well represented in the order parameters.

Our Monte Carlo results can also be compared with the Landau theory analysis presented in Sec. IV. As discussed above, both approaches yield continuous transitions between the paramagnetic phase and the magnetically ordered phases, while the transition between the two distinct magnetic phases (A2A_{2} and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2}) observed for Jz±<1/2J_{z\pm}<1/\sqrt{2} is identified as first order. The evolution of the order parameters shown in Figs. 6(b) and (c) near the continuous transition at Tc2T_{\mathrm{c2}} closely resembles the corresponding Landau transition in Fig. 4(c). However, the critical exponent β\beta in the power law ⟨mA2⟩∝(Tc2−T)β\langle m_{A_{2}}\rangle\propto(T_{\mathrm{c2}}-T)^{\beta} differs from the value predicted by Landau theory, as expected below the upper critical dimension. The behavior near the low-temperature transition at Tc1T_{\mathrm{c1}}, between the A2A_{2} and A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phases [Figs. 6(b) and (c)], can be qualitatively described by the Landau transition shown in Fig. 4(f). For Jz±>1/2J_{z\pm}>1/\sqrt{2}, the evolution of the order parameters [Figs. 7(b) and (c)] is similar to that captured by the Landau transition in Fig. 4(d), where the EE order parameter dominates near the phase transition, while the A2A_{2} order parameter becomes comparable only deeper in the ordered phase.

VI Spin nematic phase

In this section, we present a detailed discussion of the nematic phase found in the vicinity of the point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}. We discuss the emergence of additional symmetries at this point and identify dual models that consequently realize analogous ground states at low temperatures. We illustrate how the ground-state configurations of the nematic state can be explicitly constructed, and demonstrate that these can be classified according to their total magnetization. We then present a detailed Monte Carlo analysis illustrating how the nematic phase is reached from higher temperatures, and discuss the correlation functions and irrep-magnitude distributions measured in this phase.

VI.1 Additional symmetries at Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2}

The point Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2} plays a special role along the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line, with no conventional magnetic order detected down to the lowest temperatures [36]. At this point, the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) has a subextensive number of additional exact symmetries that prevent dipole ordering throughout the whole system. To discuss the symmetries and construct the ground-state manifold, it is convenient to first discuss the case Jz±=−1/2J_{z\pm}=-1/\sqrt{2}, which is dual to Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} [5, 30]. At this point, the Hamiltonian takes the simplified form

ℋnem<=J2​∑⊠(s0x​s1x+s2x​s3x+s0y​s2y+s1y​s3y+s0z​s3z+s1z​s2z)\mathcal{H}_{\rm nem}^{<}=J_{2}\sum_{\boxtimes}(s_{0}^{x}s_{1}^{x}+s_{2}^{x}s_{3}^{x}+s_{0}^{y}s_{2}^{y}+s_{1}^{y}s_{3}^{y}+s_{0}^{z}s_{3}^{z}+s_{1}^{z}s_{2}^{z}) (33)

in the global basis defined in Appendix A. Here, J2=3​Jz​z<0J_{2}=3J_{zz}<0, and the global spin components sμαs_{\mu}^{\alpha} are obtained using Eq. (43). We refer to the Hamiltonian in Eq. (33) as the “nematic” Hamiltonian ℋnem<\mathcal{H}^{<}_{\rm nem}, where << signifies the negative sign of the coupling Jz±J_{z\pm}. To expose the additional symmetry realized by the nematic Hamiltonian, we first note that the pyrochlore lattice can be constructed as a set of nonoverlapping chains in three possible ways; (i) the first is obtained by considering chains running along the (110) and (11¯\bar{1}0) directions, (ii) the second way is by considering chains running along the (011) and (011¯\bar{1}) directions, (iii) and the last possible way is by considering chains running along the (101) and (101¯\bar{1}) directions.1414 14 We note that these three ways are related by a cubic C3C_{3} symmetry. In each of these cases, a chain is composed of only two specific sublattice sites, e.g., the chains running along the (110) direction are composed of sublattice sites μ=0\mu=0 and μ=1\mu=1.

The nematic Hamiltonian consists of three different terms with Ising-type interactions along the three different cubic axes in the global basis, namely an xx term J2​∑⊠s0x​s1x+s2x​s3xJ_{2}\sum_{\boxtimes}s_{0}^{x}s_{1}^{x}+s_{2}^{x}s_{3}^{x}, a yy term J2​∑⊠s0y​s2y+s1y​s3yJ_{2}\sum_{\boxtimes}s_{0}^{y}s_{2}^{y}+s_{1}^{y}s_{3}^{y}, and a zz term J2​∑⊠s0z​s3z+s1z​s2zJ_{2}\sum_{\boxtimes}s_{0}^{z}s_{3}^{z}+s_{1}^{z}s_{2}^{z}. On the level of a single tetrahedron, each of these terms describes a pair-wise ferromagnetic (recall that J2<0J_{2}<0) interaction between the global Cartesian components of the spins on two perpendicular bonds of a single tetrahedron. In the full lattice, each of these sets of interactions defines a system of nonoverlapping infinite spin chains, corresponding to the three ways in which the pyrochlore can be constructed as mentioned above. The decomposition of the nematic Hamiltonian into the xx, yy, and zz terms results in an additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry on every spin chain over a fixed cartesian component of the spins. Focusing on the xx term, for example, the Hamiltonian is invariant under the transformation (s0x,s1x)→−(s0x,s1x)(s_{0}^{x},s_{1}^{x})\to-(s_{0}^{x},s_{1}^{x}), with the spins in sublattices 00 and 11 lying on a chain along the (110) direction. As these additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry transformations only involve a subset of the spins in the lattice, we identify these as subsystem symmetries.

The subsystem symmetries also result in an enlarged ground-state manifold. Indeed, since each spin chain is associated with a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry, there are of the order of 6​L26L^{2} additional subsystem symmetries on the system. These imply that the ground-state manifold of the system must present a similar number of ground-state configurations, resulting in a subextensive ground-state manifold. This subextensive degeneracy can exposed by studying the spectrum of the interaction matrix Ji​jα​βJ_{ij}^{\alpha\beta} associated to the nematic Hamiltonian in reciprocal space.1515 15 For a general bilinear spin models, a Hamiltonian can be rewritten in the form ℋ=12​∑i,jsiα​Ji​jα​β​sjβ\mathcal{H}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}s_{i}^{\alpha}J_{ij}^{\alpha\beta}s_{j}^{\beta}. Figure 9 illustrates the energy bands of the interaction matrix along two high-symmetry paths. We note that, in the [h​h​ℓ][hh\ell] plane [Fig. 9(a)], the lowest-energy band is completely flat, whereas it becomes dispersive in the [h​k​0][hk0] plane [Fig. 9(b)]. From a self-consistent Gaussian approximation (a soft-spin approximation where the spin-length constraint is fulfilled on average in the system) [73, 74, 75, 30], this degeneracy in the lowest-energy bands implies that there are 𝒪⁡(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}) spin modes in the ground-state manifold, agreeing with the 6​L26L^{2} additional subsystem symmetries ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} present in the model with Jz±=−1/2J_{z\pm}=-1/\sqrt{2}. Furthermore, due to the duality of the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) under the sign change of the Jz±J_{z\pm} coupling [5], all the properties we have discussed for the Hamiltonian ℋnem<\mathcal{H}^{<}_{\rm nem}, where Jz±=−1/2J_{z\pm}=-1/\sqrt{2}, are also applicable to its dual, namely ℋnem>\mathcal{H}^{>}_{\rm nem}, where Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}.1616 16 In particular, the spectrum of the interaction matrix possess the same form.

The spectrum of the interaction matrix shown in Fig. 9 exposes an additional symmetry of the system: the bands of the interaction matrix are symmetric about the zero-energy line. This symmetry implies that the subsystem symmetries and ground-state degeneracy realized in the nematic Hamiltonians ℋnem<\mathcal{H}^{<}_{\rm nem} and ℋnem>\mathcal{H}^{>}_{\rm nem} must also hold for their inverse additives −ℋnem<-\mathcal{H}^{<}_{\rm nem} and −ℋnem>-\mathcal{H}^{>}_{\rm nem}. The additional symmetry of the spectrum is also reflected in the irreps’ energies. Indeed, we identify two sets of degenerate irreps with opposite energies, each one containing six out of the twelve degrees of freedom encoded in the irreps; one with aA​2=aE=aT1−=3​Jz​za_{A2}=a_{E}=a_{T_{1-}}=3J_{zz} and the other aT2=aT1+=−3​Jz​za_{T_{2}}=a_{T_{1+}}=-3J_{zz}. Hence, we can identify the six negative-energy bands in Fig. 9 with the six negative-energy modes, while the positive-energy bands link to the six positive-energy irreps. Depending on the sign of Jz​zJ_{zz}, the negative-energy modes are identified with A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} for Jz​z<0J_{zz}<0 and with T1−⊕T2T_{1-}\oplus T_{2} for Jz​z>0J_{zz}>0. Below, we demonstrate that the point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line realizes an exact nematic point. The duality involving the Jz​zJ_{zz} sign, combined with the duality relating positive and negative Jz±J_{z\pm} regions, allows us then to expose four exact nematic points, two on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} degenerate line and two on the T1−⊕T2T_{1-}\oplus T_{2} degenerate plane, as summarized in Tab. 1.

VI.2 Characterization of ground-state manifold

The presence of the additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsytem symmetries has important consequences for the single-tetrahedron irreps. These symmetries provide an exact relation between the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} spin configuration and the T1−T_{1-} irreps. At the nematic point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}, the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} configurations with the highest-entropy contribution consist of six antiferromagnetic configurations, for example

𝐒0\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{0} =2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y−𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}-\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, 𝐒1\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{1} =−2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y−𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}-\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, (34)
𝐒2\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{2} =−2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, 𝐒3\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{3} =2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S.\displaystyle=\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,. (35)

on a single tetrahedron, as sketched in Fig. 10(a). On the other hand, the T1−T_{1-} subspace consists of six splayed ferromagnetic states, such as

𝐒0\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{0} =−2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, 𝐒1\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{1} =2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, (36)
𝐒2\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{2} =−2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, 𝐒3\displaystyle\mathbf{S}_{3} =2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\displaystyle=\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,, (37)

shown in Fig. 10(b).

We note that in these two configurations the spins 𝐒0\mathbf{S}_{0} and 𝐒1\mathbf{S}_{1} are inverted, whereas the remaining spins 𝐒2\mathbf{S}_{2} and 𝐒3\mathbf{S}_{3} possess the same orientation. The agreement between the spin configurations in sublattices μ=2\mu=2 and μ=3\mu=3 is associated with the additional subsystem ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} symmetry. In other words, starting from a single-tetrahedron A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} spin configuration, the application of a ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetry on the spin chain containing sites μ=0\mu=0 and μ=1\mu=1 yields a single-tetrahedron T1−T_{1-} state, illustrated in Fig. 10(b). In more general terms, each of the six states of the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} subspace are mapped by the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetry to a unique T1−T_{1-} state. The fact that the relation between these spin configurations arises from an exact symmetry at Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} implies that the T1−T_{1-} irrep presents the exact same entropy and therefore must be present at higher temperatures, as also confirmed by our Monte Carlo results discussed in Sec. VI.3.1717 17 The additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetry at the point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} yields a low-temperature phase featuring a reappearance of the T1−T_{1-} irreps, which contrasts with the depopulation of the T1−T_{1-} mode throughout the rest of the phase diagram.

Beyond the single-tetrahedron level, the fact that the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} and T1−T_{1-} modes feature the same 𝐒2\mathbf{S}_{2} and 𝐒3\mathbf{S}_{3}, but different 𝐒0\mathbf{S}_{0} and 𝐒1\mathbf{S}_{1}, allows us to tile single tetrahedra with different spin configurations, effectively constructing full spin configurations in the entire lattice. Following this construction results in spin configurations of ordered chains with each tetrahedron realizing either a A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} or T1−T_{1-} state. This leads to a multitude of full-lattice spin configurations which, in general, do not preserve translational symmetry. Due to the subsystem symmetries, each chain of spins is independent from the others, suppressing any long-range dipolar order. As a consequence, time reversal symmetry is preserved, but the preferred directions of the spins break the rotational symmetry of the microscopic Hamiltonian, resulting in a spin nematic state at low temperatures.

Let us now use the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetries to identify and characterize the spin configuration in the ground-state manifold. As a starting point, consider the Hamiltonian ℋnem<\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{nem}}^{<} in Eq. (33). In this case, the T1−T_{1-} irrep describes a collinear ferromagnetic spin configuration. Taking one of the three cubic domains, say the zz direction, we can explicitly construct the ground-state manifold. Consider the fully aligned state with all chains pointing along the +z+z direction with magnetization 4​L3​S4L^{3}S, corresponding to all tetrahedra being in the +z+z component of the T1−T_{1-} mode. The application of the ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetries along the chains results in full-lattice configurations belonging to distinct magnetization sectors. Each magnetization sector has a total magnetization of Mn=(4​L3−4​L​n)​SM_{n}=(4L^{3}-4Ln)S, obtained by flipping the zz components of the spins in nn randomly selected spin chains of the fully aligned configuration. Following this procedure until all spin chains have been flipped, results in the fully aligned state along the −z-z direction, which features all the tetrahedra in the −z-z component of the T1−T_{1-} mode. Each magnetization sector can be characterized by the number of flipped spin chains nn, which varies from 0 in the fully aligned state along the +z+z direction to 2​L22L^{2} for the fully aligned state along the −z-z direction.

This identification allows us to count the number of microstates per magnetization sector

Ωn=(2​L2n),\Omega_{n}=\begin{pmatrix}2L^{2}\\ n\end{pmatrix}, (38)

contributing to the degeneracy of the ground state, see Fig. 11(a), and leading to a subextensive residual entropy of

𝒮=ln⁡(3​∑n=02​L2Ωn)=2​L2​ln⁡2+ln⁡3,\mathcal{S}=\ln\left(3\sum_{n=0}^{2L^{2}}\Omega_{n}\right)=2L^{2}\ln 2+\ln{3}\,, (39)

where the multiplicative factor 33 accounts for the three cubic directions.

The magnetization sector with the largest number of microstates is reached when half of the spin chains are flipped, i.e., for n=L2n=L^{2}, and the total magnetization of the system vanishes. All other sectors have a nonvanishing total magnetization. We note that time reversal symmetry links positive and negative magnetization sectors of the ground-state manifold, enforcing the magnetization to be an odd function with center n=L2n=L^{2}, as shown in Fig. 11(a), and proved by the relation M2​L2−n=−4​L​(L2−n)​S=−MnM_{2L^{2}-n}=-4L(L^{2}-n)S=-M_{n}. The microstate degeneracy is an even function around the point n=L2n=L^{2}, with Ω2​L2−n=Ωn\Omega_{2L^{2}-n}=\Omega_{n}. The magnetization distribution shown in Fig. 11(b) is peaked around M=0M=0. As the thermodynamic limit is approached, the width of the distribution decreases proportionally to 1/L1/L, while the height of the peak at M=0M=0 increases as 22​L2/L2^{2L^{2}}/L. In this limit, the distribution converges to a delta-like form centered at zero magnetization, indicating that time-reversal symmetry remains unbroken in the ground state at the nematic point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}.

A representative ground-state configuration of the nematic Hamiltonian ℋnem<\mathcal{H}^{<}_{\rm nem} with zero magnetization (n=L2n=L^{2}) is displayed in Fig. 11(c), where all tetrahedra are in a collinear antiferromagnetic configuration. In Fig. 11(d), we provide the equivalent dual configuration, obtained for the dual nematic Hamiltonian ℋnem>\mathcal{H}^{>}_{\rm nem} for Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}. The duality preserves the degeneracy counting and the symmetry, which remains valid also in the ℋnem>\mathcal{H}^{>}_{\rm nem} case. The duality transformation connecting the positive and negative Jz±J_{z\pm} cases acts as a C2C_{2} rotation about the local 𝐳μ\mathbf{z}_{\mu} axes. An example is shown in Fig. 11(c)-(d), with spin transforming

𝐒0=S​𝐞z↦2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y−𝐞z3​S,𝐒1=S​𝐞z↦−2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y−𝐞z3​S,𝐒2=−S​𝐞z↦−2​𝐞x+2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,𝐒3=−S​𝐞z↦2​𝐞x−2​𝐞y+𝐞z3​S,\begin{split}\mathbf{S}_{0}&=S\mathbf{e}_{z}\mapsto\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}-\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,,\\ \mathbf{S}_{1}&=S\mathbf{e}_{z}\mapsto\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}-\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,,\\ \mathbf{S}_{2}&=-S\mathbf{e}_{z}\mapsto\frac{-2\mathbf{e}_{x}+2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,,\\ \mathbf{S}_{3}&=-S\mathbf{e}_{z}\mapsto\frac{2\mathbf{e}_{x}-2\mathbf{e}_{y}+\mathbf{e}_{z}}{3}S\,,\end{split} (40)

from the Jz±=−1/2J_{z\pm}=-1/\sqrt{2} spin configuration on the left-hand side to Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} spin configuration on the right-hand side, where the spin components are expressed in the global basis defined in Appendix A.

The preceding arguments deserve an additional remark. As discussed in the previous subsection, the interaction-matrix band analysis in Sec. VI.1 reveals flat planes rather than flat bands among the low-energy modes, as shown in Fig. 9. This structure implies a scaling of the ground-state degeneracy as 𝒪⁡(L2)\mathcal{O}(L^{2}), consistent with the subextensive residual entropy in Eq. (39). However, the states considered in the above reasoning do not exhaust the full set of energetically degenerate states. In particular, the pure A2A_{2} all-in-all-out and the EE long-range-ordered states also belong to the degenerate manifold, yet they were not included in our counting. The reason is that their degeneracy is only of order 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1). These long-range-ordered configurations correspond to the band-touching points at the Γ\Gamma point in Fig. 9, which do not contribute (sub-)extensively. Thus, our estimate captures those states that are entropically relevant, yielding a subextensive degeneracy that governs the physics in the thermodynamic limit.

VI.3 Classical Monte Carlo at Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2}

In this subsection, we present the finite-temperature behavior of the system at the nematic point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} obtained via classical Monte Carlo. Figure 12 illustrates the specific heat, the nematic and magnetic order parameters, and the spin structure factor obtained at two distinct temperatures. The finite-temperature behavior of the specific heat shows a strong first-order transition from the paramagnetic phase to the spin nematic phase, as visible in Fig. 12(a), where the dashed line signals the transition temperature TcT_{\rm c}. Below the transition temperature, the nematic order parameter in Eq. (30) becomes nonzero, keeps on increasing with decreasing temperature, and approaches saturation in the limit T→0T\to 0, see Fig. 12(b). As discussed in the previous subsections, since no dipole ordering is present, all magnetic order parameters vanish, implying the absence of magnetic long-range order at low temperature, as indicated by the sublattice magnetic order parameter shown in Fig. 12(c). The lack of magnetic long-range order is further supported by the absence of magnetic Bragg peaks in the spin static structure factor, as illustrated in Figs. 12(d)-(e). Instead of sharp peaks, the correlation functions develop continuous lines of scattering, connecting points of high symmetry, similar to the ones observed in the nematic phase at finite temperatures above the A2⊕T1−⊕T2A_{2}\oplus T_{1-}\oplus T_{2} line [30]. The observation of such continuous features in the spin static structure factor is consistent with the subextensive degeneracy present in the nematic manifold. At temperatures above the critical temperature, where no symmetry breaking has taken place, these continuous lines of scattering are broader, and the system has access to all symmetry sectors. The broadness of these features is associated with thermal fluctuations, signaling the nonvanishing thermal population of high-energy modes. As the temperature is decreased below the critical temperature, the system selects one of the three cubic C3C_{3} symmetry sectors while heavily suppressing high-energy modes, resulting in sharper features.1818 18 As discussed in Ref. [30], the structure factor for a single C3C_{3} symmetry sector would only display continuous lines along one cartesian axis.

In Sec. VI.2, the ground-state manifold of the nematic phase is described in terms of irreps, where it was found that the high-entropy A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} single-tetrahedron configurations transform into single-tetrahedron T1−T_{1-} configurations by means of the additional exact subsystem symmetries. Tiling the lattice with these single-tetrahedron configuration leads to a multitude of full-lattice ground-state spin configurations, which do not exhibit magnetic long-range order. We now test the robustness of this construction at finite temperatures by inspecting the irrep-magnitude distributions of the A2A_{2}, EE, and T1−T_{1-} in the T<TcT<T_{\mathrm{c}} temperature regime obtained from Monte Carlo simulations. Using the mixing angles θ\theta and ϕ\phi defined in Eq. (10), we identify two “domains” of spin configurations on the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} sphere at low temperatures, see Fig. 13. The region close to the equator (θ>π/4\theta>\pi/4) in the distribution shown in Fig. 13(b) corresponds to single tetrahedra whose spin configurations are mainly described by the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E configurations. In the irrep-magnitude distribution, the white dashed line marks the mixing angle ϕ\phi between the A2A_{2} and the EE irreps predicted by a classical low-temperature expansion, see Sec. III. We note that the domain with a high A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E irrep contribution is centered around the value predicted by the classical low-temperature expansion at Jz±≶1/2J_{z\pm}\lessgtr 1/\sqrt{2}, supporting the assumption that the construction of the ground-state manifold presented in the previous subsection is still valid at finite temperatures in the nematic phase. The second region where most single-tetrahedron configuration cluster is observed near the θ=0\theta=0 point. Spin configurations near this point are mainly described by a T1−T_{1-} irreps, as underlined by the intense area around θ=0\theta=0 (θ<π/4\theta<\pi/4) in Fig. 13(b). The T1−T_{1-} mode consists of six single-tetrahedron states, such as the one in Eqs. (36) and (37), related by C3C_{3} and time reversal symmetry, and corresponding to the xx,yy, and zz components of the irrep. Depending on the symmetry-breaking pattern of the cubic symmetry, all the tetrahedra in the T1−T_{1-} mode select one out of the three xx, yy, or zz components of the irrep. Due to the additional subsystem symmetries at the nematic point, the T1−T_{1-} selected component matches the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} mode, as described in Sec. VI.2. Hence, it is possible to tile a full lattice configuration consisting of tetrahedra in the T1−T_{1-} or A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} modes. For additional details on the T1−T_{1-} mode in the nematic phase, we refer to Appendix G.

This irrep-magnitude distribution obtained for the nematic phase strongly differs from the one shown in Fig. 6(e) for the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} low-temperature phase, where all the irreps cluster close to the equator. In the case of the nematic phase, the presence of the T1−T_{1-} irrep in the distribution is characteristic for the nematic phase. It is directly related to the subsystem symmetries discussed in Sec. VI.1. Due to these additional symmetries, the energetically degenerate T1−T_{1-} mode also becomes entropically equivalent to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} irrep, see Sec. VI.2. As a consequence, the T1−T_{1-} mode appears in the ground-state manifold, as observed in Fig. 13(b).

VI.4 Classical Monte Carlo slightly away from Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2}

We conclude this section by presenting Monte Carlo results slightly away from the nematic point Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}. As a representative example, we show the data for Jz±=0.74J_{z\pm}=0.74, but the same qualitative behavior is observed in a range of values 0.5≲Jz±≲0.90.5\lesssim J_{z\pm}\lesssim 0.9. The behavior of the system is summarized in Fig. 14. The specific heat [Fig. 14(a)] shows a sharp peak that can be associated with a first-order transition. At the transition temperature Tc2T_{\rm c2}, marked by a dashed line, the magnitude of the nematic order parameter jumps, corroborating the first-order transition scenario, as displayed in Fig. 14(b). Both the specific heat and the nematic order parameter appear to evolve continuously toward a unit value as the temperature decreases. However, in contrast to the situation at the exact nematic point [cf. Fig. 12(c)], the sublattice magnetic order parameter for Jz±≠1/2J_{z\pm}\neq 1/\sqrt{2}, shown in Fig. 14(c), starts to increase below a certain temperature, marking the onset of a 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 magnetic long-range-ordered phase. This low-temperature ordered phase corresponds to the mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase predicted by classical low-temperature expansion and is included in the antiferromagnetic sector of the ground-state manifold of the nematic phase. We note, however, that the transition temperature Tc1T_{\mathrm{c}1} at which the system crosses from the nematic phase to the long-range order A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} is strongly renormalized by size effects: as the system size increases, the temperature at which the sublattice magnetic order parameter becomes nonzero also increases significantly. This pronounced finite-size effect may originate from the abundance of states that are nearly degenerate in both energy and entropy. Here, it complicates the determination of the nature of the transition between the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} order at low temperatures and the spin-nematic order at intermediate temperatures from the numerical data. However, the analytical solution at Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2} allows us to infer that at least one phase transition must occur between the nematic phase and the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} magnetic phase somewhere in the phase diagram. This follows from the fact that time-reversal symmetry remains unbroken above the exact nematic point at all temperatures, whereas the numerical data clearly indicate a time-reversal-symmetry-broken state for Jz±≳0.9J_{z\pm}\gtrsim 0.9 at sufficiently low temperatures. We therefore interpret the features observed in the sublattice order parameter at low temperatures as evidence of a true phase transition, even though, based on the numerics alone, they cannot be unambiguously distinguished from a crossover.

To estimate the transition temperature, we identify the local maximum of the sublattice-order-parameter susceptibility for different system sizes. Extrapolation to the thermodynamic limit then provides an estimate for Tc1T_{\mathrm{c1}}, indicated by the dashed line in Fig. 14. This estimate suggests the existence of a finite temperature window in which the nematic phase is realized. A more precise determination of Tc1T_{\mathrm{c1}} would require a more extensive study, including simulations of larger system sizes.

VII Discussion and conclusion

In this work, we consider a specific realization of the most general bilinear nearest-neighbor spin model on the pyrochlore lattice. The model is parametrized by the interaction coupling Jz±J_{z\pm}, which tunes along the line in parameter space where an exact ground-state energy degeneracy among the A2A_{2}, EE, and T1−T_{1-} states occurs. Using large-scale classical Monte Carlo simulations, we show that this model exhibits a rich phase diagram, featuring two distinct 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 magnetic long-range-ordered phases and a novel nematic phase emerging near |Jz±|=1/2|J_{z\pm}|=1/\sqrt{2}. For |Jz±|≲0.5|J_{z\pm}|\lesssim 0.5, classical Monte Carlo simulations reveal two distinct 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases; a intermediate-temperature A2A_{2} phase and a low-temperatures mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase. In the mixed phase, the order parameters of both the A2A_{2} and EE are nonvanishing and the precise single-tetrahedron spin configuration is parametrized by a mixing angle ϕ⁡(Jz±)\phi(J_{z\pm}) between the two orders. In contrast, for |Jz±|≳0.9|J_{z\pm}|\gtrsim 0.9, a A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} mixed 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phase is realized already right below the high-temperature paramagnetic phase and remains stable down to the lowest temperatures considered. The coexistence of the A2A_{2} and EE ordered phases in the mixed phase is possible only because of their ground-state energy degeneracy, which arises from the specific model considered, and the compatibility of the order parameters describing these phases [51]. Using a classical-low temperature expansion, we demonstrate that the selection of the mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase is a consequence of a thermal order-by-disorder phenomenon [18, 24, 37, 20], where the mixing angle ϕ⁡(Jz±)\phi(J_{z\pm}) parametrizes the configurations in the 2-sphere describing the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E set of states with the highest entropy contribution. Interestingly, we show that the evolution of the order-by-disorder-selected state as a function of the coupling Jz±J_{z\pm} presents a discontinuity at Jz±∼1.262J_{z\pm}\sim 1.262, where the spin orientation of the state with the highest entropy abruptly changes. We further show that the rich behavior of this model, including the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phases realized, the qualitative behavior of the order parameters, and the order of the symmetry-breaking transition between these phases, is qualitatively captured by a Landau theory constructed using the order parameters of the A2A_{2} and EE phases. Although the realization of the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} mixed 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 phase falls within the traditional paradigm of the irrep used to described the low-temperature phases in the general bilinear nearest-neighbor on the pyrochlore lattice [32, 31], it constitutes the first theoretical example of a low-temperature phase where more than one irrep is present in an ordered phase down to the lowest temperatures. We note that a similar experimental proposal for a mixed state was provided in Ref. [76] for Yb2​Ti2​O7\rm Yb_{2}Ti_{2}O_{7}, a compound which lies in close proximity to the EE-T1−T_{1-} boundary. In this case however, classical Monte Carlo simulations of the classical model reveal either an EE phase or a T1−T_{1-} phase [77].

For Jz±J_{z\pm} in the vicinity of Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}, our classical Monte Carlo simulations detect a nematic phase separated by a first-order phase transition from the paramagnetic phase. At Jz±=1/2J_{z\pm}=1/\sqrt{2}, the model acquires additional ℤ2\mathbb{Z}_{2} subsystem symmetries, where the sign of a cartesian component of the spins in the global basis can be flipped along spin chains which wrap around the system. In the nematic phase, the single-tetrahedron spin configurations are described by either a mixed A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2}, or a T1−T_{1-} spin configuration. We demonstrate that these subsystem symmetries result in a subextensive degeneracy in the ground-state manifold and prevent the formation of any type of dipolar long-range order phase down to the lowest temperatures. We show that the stability of this nematic phase is not limited to the Jz±=±1/2J_{z\pm}=\pm 1/\sqrt{2} points, but presents a cone of stability extending both in temperature and parameter space. Furthermore, we have identified two additional models which are dual to the nematic Hamiltonians, and therefore present equivalent thermodynamic signatures where a low-temperature nematic phase is realized. As a last remark, we note that the ground-state manifold of the nematic phase identified in this work can be mapped into the so-called densely-packed monopole manifold, realized in a four-body-term Ising Hamiltonian [78, 79]. Indeed, the four-body-term Hamiltonian studied in Refs. [78, 79] presents a similar subsystem symmetry as the one realized for the nematic model.

Altogether, our work elucidates the rich behavior resulting from strong competition between distinct magnetic phases, where phenomena like thermal order-by-disorder and nematic phases can be realized in the pyrochlore lattice. It would be of great interest to study how quantum fluctuation may modify the observed phenomena. The introduction of these effects may result in the stabilization of distinct phases at higher temperatures [24], and in the more extreme cases even prevent the formation of long-range order [35]. On the other hand, we expect that no conventional magnetic order is observed for the nematic points, where the additional subsystem symmetries remain valid symmetries in the quantum model.

In this appendix, we provide details on the basis conventions employed in the main text. Moreover, we explicitly report the single-tetrahedron irrep in terms of spin components.

𝐞x=(1,0,0)𝐞y=(0,1,0),𝐞z=(0,0,1).\mathbf{e}_{x}=(1,0,0)\,\quad\mathbf{e}_{y}=(0,1,0)\,,\quad\mathbf{e}_{z}=(0,0,1)\,. (42)
