𝐒μ=∑α=x,y,zsμα​𝐞αwithsμα=𝐒μ⋅𝐞α,\mathbf{S}_{\mu}=\sum_{\alpha=x,y,z}s_{\mu}^{\alpha}\mathbf{e}_{\alpha}\quad\mathrm{with}\quad s_{\mu}^{\alpha}=\mathbf{S}_{\mu}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{\alpha}\,, (43)

where the calligraphic notation denotes the spin components in the global coordinate frame. Equivalently, in the local basis, spins are decomposed as

𝐒μ=Sμx​𝐱μ+Sμy​𝐲μ+Sμz​𝐳μ=(𝐒μ⋅𝐱μ)​𝐱μ+(𝐒μ⋅𝐲μ)​𝐲μ+(𝐒μ⋅𝐳μ)​𝐳μ,\begin{split}\mathbf{S}_{\mu}&=S_{\mu}^{x}\mathbf{x}_{\mu}+S_{\mu}^{y}\mathbf{y}_{\mu}+S_{\mu}^{z}\mathbf{z}_{\mu}\\ &=(\mathbf{S_{\mu}\cdot\mathbf{x}_{\mu}})\mathbf{x}_{\mu}+(\mathbf{S_{\mu}\cdot\mathbf{y}_{\mu}})\mathbf{y}_{\mu}+(\mathbf{S_{\mu}\cdot\mathbf{z}_{\mu}})\mathbf{z}_{\mu}\,,\end{split} (44)

where the standard mathematical font is related to the spin components is the local basis notation, since it is mostly used throughout the paper. For example, the Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) contains spin components expressed in the local coordinate frame. However, the same Hamiltonian can be expressed in the global basis, with interaction parameters {J1,J2,J3,J4}\{J_{1},J_{2},J_{3},J_{4}\}, or in a coordinate-free notation with couplings {JH,JIs,JDM,JPD}\{J_{\mathrm{H}},J_{\mathrm{Is}},J_{\mathrm{DM}},J_{\mathrm{PD}}\} [43].

The Hamiltonian in Eq. (1) is reformulated as a sum of single-tetrahedron Hamiltionians ℋ⊠\mathcal{H}_{\boxtimes}

ℋ=∑⊠ℋ⊠,\mathcal{H}=\sum_{\boxtimes}\mathcal{H}_{\boxtimes}\,,

where the sum runs on every tetrahedron on the pyrochlore lattice. The single-tetrahedron Hamiltonian can be formulated in terms of single-tetrahedron irreps 𝐦I\mathbf{m}_{I} and their associated energy aIa_{I},

ℋ⊠=12​(aA2​mA22+aE​𝐦E2+aT2​𝐦T22+aT1,ice​𝐦T1,ice2CLOSEOPEN+aT1,planar​𝐦T1,planar2+aT1,mix​𝐦T1,ice⋅𝐦T1,planar),\begin{split}\mathcal{H}_{\boxtimes}&=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{A_{2}}m_{A_{2}}^{2}+a_{E}\mathbf{m}_{E}^{2}+a_{T_{2}}\mathbf{m}_{T_{2}}^{2}+a_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}\mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}^{2}\right.\\ &+\left.a_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}\mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}^{2}+a_{T_{1,\mathrm{mix}}}\mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}\cdot\mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}\right)\,,\end{split} (45)

where the aT1,mix=−4​Jz±a_{T_{1,\mathrm{mix}}}=-4J_{z\pm} is the energy associated to the mixing term between the T1,iceT_{1,\mathrm{ice}} and T1,planarT_{1,\mathrm{planar}} irreps. The irreps are linear combinations of the single-tetrahedron spin components. In Table 2, each irrep is reported together with its energy and its expression in terms of spin components in the local basis. The mixed T1T_{1} irreps can be rotated into two new irreps T1±T_{1\pm} to suppress any mixing terms between the resulting T1T_{1} irreps, namely

(𝐦T1−𝐦T1+)=(cos⁡αmixsin⁡αmix−sin⁡αmixcos⁡αmix)​(𝐦T1,ice𝐦T1,planar),\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{m}_{T_{1-}}\\ \mathbf{m}_{T_{1+}}\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}\cos{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}&\sin{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}\\ -\sin{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}&\cos{\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}}\\ \end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}\\ \mathbf{m}_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}\end{pmatrix}, (46)

where the rotation angle is obtained by

tan⁡2​αmix=2​amixaT1,ice−aT1,planar=8​Jz±Jz​z+2​J±+4​J±⁣±.\tan 2\alpha_{\mathrm{mix}}=\frac{2a_{\mathrm{mix}}}{a_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}-a_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}}=\frac{8J_{z\pm}}{J_{zz}+2J_{\pm}+4J_{\pm\pm}}\,. (47)

aT1±=12​(aT1,ice+aT1,planar±(aT1,ice−aT1,planar)2+amix2),a_{T_{1\pm}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(a_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}+a_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}}\pm\sqrt{(a_{T_{1,\mathrm{ice}}}-a_{T_{1,\mathrm{planar}}})^{2}+a_{\mathrm{mix}}^{2}}\right)\,, (48)

where the T1−T_{1-} irrep is defined as the one always having the lower energy aT1−<aT1+a_{T_{1-}}<a_{T_{1+}}. In the non-Kramers case Jz±=0J_{z\pm}=0, the local zz component of the spins decouples from the local transverse components, reducing the T1±T_{1\pm} irreps to the spin-ice and planar, T1,planarT_{1,\mathrm{planar}} irreps. The T1,iceT_{1,\mathrm{ice}} spin-ice irrep consists of spins lying along the local zz direction and pointing either inward or outward the tetrahedron following the two-in-two-out rule, or ice rule. On the other hand, the T1,planarT_{1,\mathrm{planar}} irrep is a splayed ferromagnetic configurations with spins lying in their local x​yxy plane [43].

Appendix B Identification of accidental symmetry manifolds

In this appendix, we provide details on the identification of the accidental symmetry manifolds of Sec. II.1. Each spin in a tetrahedron can be expressed as a function of irreps

𝐒i=𝐒i​(mA2,𝐦E,𝐦T1−)\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathbf{S}_{i}(m_{A_{2}},\mathbf{m}_{E},\mathbf{m}_{T_{1-}})

or, equivalently, as a function of the five angles in Eq. (12),

𝐒i=𝐒i​(θ,ϕ,η,β,γ)=𝐒i​(𝝅)\mathbf{S}_{i}=\mathbf{S}_{i}(\theta,\phi,\eta,\beta,\gamma)=\mathbf{S}_{i}(\bm{\pi}) (49)

where the vector 𝝅=(θ,ϕ,η,β,γ)\bm{\pi}=(\theta,\phi,\eta,\beta,\gamma) stands as a shorthand notation for the S5S^{5} angles. Each spin in the tetrahedron must also respect the strong spin constraint

𝐒i⋅𝐒i=S2,∀i∈⊠,\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{i}=S^{2},\quad\forall i\in\boxtimes\,, (50)

leading to four different equations. However, only three of these equations are independent. In principle, these equations allow us to obtain the physically relevant configuration 𝝅0\bm{\pi}_{0} respecting both the strong constraint in Eq. (50) and the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} constraint in Eq. (8).

In case where the constraints are satisfied on entire submanifolds, i.e the S2S^{2} submanifold described by the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E subspace described in Sec. II.1, the analysis can be extended by taking into account small fluctuations around some configuration 𝝅0\bm{\pi}_{0}, keeping also in mind that all the constraints still need to be satisfied. Expanding the tetrahedron spins as

Siα​(𝝅0+δ​𝝅)≈Siα​(𝝅0)+δ​𝝅⋅∇Siα|𝝅0+𝒪⁡(δ​𝝅2),S_{i}^{\alpha}(\bm{\pi}_{0}+\delta\bm{\pi})\approx S_{i}^{\alpha}(\bm{\pi}_{0})+\delta\bm{\pi}\cdot\nabla\left.S_{i}^{\alpha}\right|_{\bm{\pi}_{0}}+\mathcal{O}(\delta\bm{\pi}^{2})\,,

with a gradient operator ∇=(∂θ,∂ϕ,∂η,∂β,∂γ)\nabla=(\partial_{\theta},\partial_{\phi},\partial_{\eta},\partial_{\beta},\partial_{\gamma}), and imposing the strong spin constraint on 𝐒i​(𝝅0+δ​𝝅)\mathbf{S}_{i}(\bm{\pi}_{0}+\delta\bm{\pi}), we get four equations of the form

δ​𝝅⋅∇(𝐒i⋅𝐒i)|𝝅0=0,\delta\bm{\pi}\cdot\left.\nabla(\mathbf{S}_{i}\cdot\mathbf{S}_{i})\right|_{\bm{\pi}_{0}}=0, (51)

where only three of them are independent [36]. For nonzero fluctuations, the system of equations in Eq. (13) could have one or more solutions in (θ,ϕ,η,β,γ)(\theta,\phi,\eta,\beta,\gamma), which correspond to a single-tetrahedron spin configuration.

Appendix C Stereographic projection

In this appendix, we present details on the stereographic projection used in the main text. A point on the unitary sphere P=(x,y,z)P=(x,y,z) is mapped to a point on the plane P′=(X,Y)P^{\prime}=(X,Y) via stereographic projection

(X,Y)=(x1+z,y1+z),(X,Y)=\left(\frac{x}{1+z},\frac{y}{1+z}\right)\,, (52)

where the north pole (0,0,1)(0,0,1) of the sphere is mapped to the origin of the plane, the equator of the sphere (x,y,0)(x,y,0) to the unitary circle on the plane, and the south pole to infinity. The stereographic projection is a conformal mapping, which preserves angles from the sphere to the plane. However, it introduces some distortion in the radial direction on the plane, enlarging the objects close to the equator.

The stereographic projection can be used to visualize the mixing between the degenerate irreps along the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line. Within the angle definitions in Eq. (12), we can define an S2S^{2} sphere parametrized by the angles (θ,ϕ)(\theta,\phi) via the absolute values of the three irreps. In this case, the sphere is reduced to the first octagon. Its north pole represents the T1−T_{1-} irreps, while the equator corresponds to the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E mixed state, with special points of only A2A_{2} and EE irreps, see Fig. 6 for an example of this mapping for an A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E phase.

The stereographic projection also helps the visualization of the degenerate A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere and its U(1) orbits of soft modes. In this case, the sphere is spanned by the angles (ϕ,η)(\phi,\eta) of Eq. (12), and we restricted the representation of the sphere to the northern hemisphere to avoid infinities due to the southern hemisphere representation, see Fig. 3(a)-(c)-(f). Nevertheless, time-reversal symmetry links states on the northern hemisphere to ones on the southern hemisphere, ensuring a complete equivalence between the two regions.

Appendix D Further details on the classical low-temperature expansion

In the main text, we discussed how the low-temperature selection of the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 state evolves as a function of the coupling parameter Jz±J_{z\pm}. In particular, we identified two high-entropy branches in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E manifold, where the highest entropy branch changes at a value Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star}. In this appendix, we numerically determine the value of Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star}. In Fig. 15, we illustrate the value of Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star} at which the two high-entropy branches have an equal entropy as a function of system size LL used to perform the calculation. A naive linear 1/L1/L fit of the different computed system sizes predicts that the Jz±⋆≃1.2624J_{z\pm}^{\star}\simeq 1.2624 in the thermodynamic limit.

The error bars in Fig. 15 are obtained as an upper limit of the Riemann-sum integration error by the product of the maximal value obtained by the entropy by the integrated function in Eq. (16), times the volume of the integration range divided by the number of 𝐪\mathbf{q} points used in a Riemann integration. We note that, for interaction parameters near to Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star} an approximately uniform entropy is measured along a continuous path in the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E sphere, see Fig. 16.

Interestingly, at Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star}, the angular difference between the two branches, i.e. ϕ1−ϕ2\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}, is approximately π/3\pi/3. Using the equations defining the angles ϕ1\phi_{1} and ϕ2\phi_{2}, namely Eq. (17) and Eq. (18), and assuming that ϕ1−ϕ2=π/3\phi_{1}-\phi_{2}=\pi/3 at Jz±⋆J_{z\pm}^{\star} we obtain the value

Jz±⋆=1+1+κ2κwithκ=tan⁡(2​arctan⁡3+112),J_{z\pm}^{\star}=\frac{1+\sqrt{1+\kappa^{2}}}{\kappa}\quad\mathrm{with}\quad\kappa=\tan\left(2\arctan\frac{\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{11}}{2}\right), (53)

yielding an approximate value of Jz±⋆≃1.26216J_{z\pm}^{\star}\simeq 1.26216, which approximates the value obtained from the finite size analysis in Fig. 15. Although the angle difference of π/3\pi/3 suggests that certain symmetry would be the driving mechanism of the entropy degeneracy between these branches, we note that the symmetries of the pyrochlore include rotations by 2​π/32\pi/3, not π/3\pi/3. We leave the study of the mechanism behind this degeneracy as future work.

Appendix E Further details on the Landau theory

In this appendix, we provide further details on the Landau theory presented in Sec. V. First, we identify all invariant terms and derive the free energy in Eq. (21). Next, we discuss the minimization of the free energy and visualize the selection of the global minimum at the phase transition from the A2A_{2} to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase. Finally, an additional analysis of the transition from the paramagnetic phase to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase and phase diagrams, similar to Fig. 4, for distinct sets of parameters is presented.

To identify the symmetry-allowed terms of the free energy in Eq. (21), we first study the action of the symmetry transformations of the tetrahedral group TdT_{d} on the irreps mA2m_{A_{2}} and 𝐦E\mathbf{m}_{E}, as shown in Table 2. The single-tetrahedron group TdT_{d} exhibits four types of symmetries: a C3C_{3} symmetry around the local ⟨111⟩\langle 111\rangle direction, C2C_{2} rotations around the global xx, yy, and zz axes, reflections σ\sigma, and an S4S_{4} symmetry consisting of reflections followed by a π/2\pi/2 rotation [5]. In addition, the time reversal symmetry τ\tau needs to be considered.

While the irreps stay invariant or assume a minus sign under most symmetry operations in Table 3, the 𝐦E\mathbf{m}_{E} irrep transforms according to

(mExmEy)→C3(cos⁡2​π​n3−sin⁡2​π​n3sin⁡2​π​n3cos⁡2​π​n3)​(mExmEy)\begin{pmatrix}m_{E}^{x}\\[2.15277pt] m_{E}^{y}\end{pmatrix}\xrightarrow{C_{3}}\begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac{2\pi n}{3}&-\sin\frac{2\pi n}{3}\\[2.15277pt] \sin\frac{2\pi n}{3}&\cos\frac{2\pi n}{3}\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}m_{E}^{x}\\[2.15277pt] m_{E}^{y}\end{pmatrix} (54)

under the C3C_{3} symmetry, corresponding to a 2​π​n/32\pi n/3 rotation (n∈{0,1,2}n\in\{0,1,2\}) in the local x​yxy plane. Following reference [51], we introduce the complex variable

mx​y=(mEx)2+(mEy)2​ei​η=|𝐦E|​ei​η​,m_{xy}=\sqrt{(m_{E}^{x})^{2}+(m_{E}^{y})^{2}}\ e^{i\eta}=|\mathbf{m}_{E}|e^{i\eta}\text{,} (55)

where |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}| corresponds to the magnitude and η\eta to the direction of the magnetic moment in the local x​yxy plane. Applying a C3C_{3} symmetry operation shifts the angle η\eta by 2​π​n/32\pi n/3 (n∈{0,1,2}n\in\{0,1,2\}). This shift imply that only terms of the form mx​ykm_{xy}^{k} are invariant under C3C_{3} if k∈3​ℤk\in 3\mathbb{Z}. In Table 4 the transformation under the tetrahedral group TdT_{d} of the real and imaginary parts of mx​ykm_{xy}^{k} is displayed.

To identify all symmetry allowed terms, we first note that the squares of the order parameters, that is mA22m_{A_{2}}^{2} and |𝐦E|2=(mEx)2+(mEy)2|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2}=(m_{E}^{x})^{2}+(m_{E}^{y})^{2} are invariant under TdT_{d}. Consequently, higher-order terms obtained from the product of these 2nd-order terms result in invariant 4th-order terms. We consider these terms to be “isotropic” in the Γ5\Gamma_{5} manifold as they obtain the same value for all the states lying on the Γ5\Gamma_{5} manifold characterized by the angle η\eta. To construct anisotropic terms, we multiply mA2m_{A_{2}} by |𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta}, where the anisotropy is reflected in the cos⁡3​η\cos{3\eta}. In particular, we note that the term mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​ηm_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta} is invariant since the minus signs in Table 3 and Table 4 under the σ\sigma, S4S_{4} and τ\tau transformations cancel out.

Following the same procedure as for the 4th order terms, we consider products of invariant 22nd and 44th order terms to obtain the allowed 66th order terms, which include both isotropic and anisotropic terms. All TdT_{d} invariant terms are summarized in Table 5.

By including all terms up to fourth order, in addition to the sixth order symmetry anisotropic and isotropic terms, |𝐦E|6​cos⁡6​η|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{6}\cos{6\eta} [5] and |𝐦E|6|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{6}, respectively,1919 19 We introduce both of these terms to ensure that the free energy does not diverge to negative infinity, yielding an unphysical behavior. we obtain the free energy of Eq. (21).

We find the value of the parameters |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}|, mA2m_{A_{2}} and η\eta as for the minimal free-energy configurations minimize Eq. (21) as a function of r0r_{0} and r1r_{1}, while leaving all other variables constant, using the Nelder-Mead (downhill simplex) method of the python scipy library [80]. We found that, for the sets of parameters considered in this work, η=n​π/3\eta=n\pi/3 where n∈{0,…,5}n\in\{0,\dots,5\}, corresponding to a ψ2\psi_{2} state. The minimization process identifies free-energy landscapes as the ones shown in Fig. 17, for the sets of parameters (r0,r1)=(0,−0.5)(r_{0},r_{1})=(0,-0.5), and (r0,r1)=(−0.05,−0.5)(r_{0},r_{1})=(-0.05,-0.5). As discussed in the main text, these parameters are located on the path 2→42\rightarrow 4 in Fig. 4(a), where a first-order transition from the A2A_{2} to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase is observed. In Fig. 17(a) the |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}| component of the global minima vanishes, meaning that the system is an A2A_{2} phase. In the immediate vicinity of the phase transition, displayed in Fig. 17(b), a separate minimum with a finite value of |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}| becomes the new global minimum, which implies that the system transitioned into an A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase. The discontinuous evolution of the global minima exposes the first-order phase transition between the two phases. Due to the high competition between the different minima, we use multiple starting points for the Nelder-Mead method, and select the solution that provides the lowest free energy.

In order to obtain the phase diagrams in Fig. 4, we identify the global minimum of the free energy in Eq. (21) for each coordinate (r1,r0)(r_{1},r_{0}) and the fixed set of parameters {r2,rx​y​z,r3,ω,r4,f6}\{r_{2},r_{xyz},r_{3},\omega,r_{4},f_{6}\}. In Fig. 18 we expand Fig. 4(d), which displays the second-order phase transition from the paramagnetic phase to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, by a logarithmic scaled plot of the order parameters in Fig. 18(b). Using the logarithmic scale we determine the dependence of the order parameters for small values of −r0-r_{0} as |𝐦E|∝−r0|\mathbf{m}_{E}|\propto\sqrt{-r_{0}} and |mA2|∝−r03|m_{A_{2}}|\propto\sqrt{-r_{0}}^{3} yielding |mA2|∝|𝐦E|3|m_{A_{2}}|\propto|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}. We note that a similar dependency of the order parameter in the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase was already found in reference [51].

The analysis presented so far is mainly focused in the set of parameters {r2,rx​y​z,r3,ω,r4,f6}\{r_{2},r_{xyz},r_{3},\omega,r_{4},f_{6}\} considered for Fig. 4 in the main text. We note however that the phases and the qualitative behavior at the phase transitions remain unchanged under different sets of parameters. In the following we analyze how the phase diagram is modified under varying the parameters rx​y​zr_{xyz} and ω\omega, and show that the qualitative behavior is kept. In particular, we consider the effect of varying the two coupling terms, namely rx​y​z​mA22​|𝐦E|2r_{xyz}m_{A_{2}}^{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2} and ω​mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η\omega m_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta}, that include both order parameters |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}| and |mA2||m_{A_{2}}|. The effect of these anisotropic two terms in the Landau theory can be understood in the following way; the rx​y​z​mA22​|𝐦E|2r_{xyz}m_{A_{2}}^{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2} is nonnegative and consequently increases the free energy, while ω​mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η\omega m_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta} always lowers the minimum of the free energy since it is the only odd term in mA2m_{A_{2}} and therefore adapts the sign to be negative. As a result we interpret rx​y​z​mA22​|𝐦E|2r_{xyz}m_{A_{2}}^{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2} as a term that suppresses the coupling between the order parameters and ω​mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η\omega m_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta} as coupling-enhancing.

In Fig. 19(a)-(b) we illustrate the magnitudes of |𝐦E||\mathbf{m}_{E}| and |mA2||m_{A_{2}}| for the case ω≫rx​y​z\omega\gg r_{xyz}. Consequently, the term rx​y​z​mA22​|𝐦E|2r_{xyz}m_{A_{2}}^{2}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{2} is suppressed relative to ω​mA2​|𝐦E|3​cos⁡3​η\omega m_{A_{2}}|\mathbf{m}_{E}|^{3}\cos{3\eta} leading to a strong coupling between the order parameters, which results in a larger magnitude of the order parameters in the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase compared to Fig. 4. Additionally, the phase transition from the A2A_{2} to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase in Fig. 19(d) takes place for larger values of r0r_{0} and displays a discontinuous upward jump in |mA2||m_{A_{2}}| compared to Fig. 4(e).

In the case ω≪rx​y​z\omega\ll r_{xyz}, shown in Fig. 20, the magnitudes of order parameters are smaller compared to Fig. 4 with |mA2||m_{A_{2}}| almost vanishing, while the phase transition from the A2A_{2} to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase in Fig. 20(d) exhibits a small downward jump in mA2m_{A_{2}}.

As previously mentioned, the general characteristics of the phase transitions discussed in Sec. V remain unchanged under the different sets of parameters: the transitions of the paramagnet to the A2A_{2} phase and the paramagnet to the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase are both of second order, and the transitions from A2A_{2} to A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} display a second-order phase transition with the direction of the jump in |mA2||m_{A_{2}}| depending on the values of the parameters. This observation implies that the general features discussed in the main text are qualitatively preserved for a variety of interaction parameters {r2,rx​y​z,r3,r4,ω,f6}\{r_{2},r_{xyz},r_{3},r_{4},\omega,f_{6}\}, which appear to be relevant for the model describing the A2⊕E⊕T1−A_{2}\oplus E\oplus T_{1-} line.

Appendix F Further details on A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} detection from Monte Carlo data

In this appendix, we provide details on the detection of the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase, in particular, how to determine whether the components of the EE phase are ψ2\psi_{2} or ψ3\psi_{3}. We used the ⟨mE​6⟩\langle m_{E6}\rangle parameter defined in Eq. (27) to determine the nature of the EE components in the 𝐪=0\mathbf{q}=0 A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E phase. Our simulations show that, throughout the Jz±J_{z\pm} range, whenever the A2⊕EA_{2}\oplus E phase is realized, the ⟨mE​6⟩\langle m_{E6}\rangle parameter becomes positive, exposing the nature of the mixed state as the A2⊕ψ2A_{2}\oplus\psi_{2} phase.
